claim: Vilya is a novel meiotic gene that encodes a protein with homology to Zip3-like proteins.
source: Here we report a novel meiotic gene, vilya, which encodes a protein with homology to Zip3-like proteins shown to determine DSB fate in other organisms.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, and the manuscript provides structural analysis showing RING domain, coiled-coil domain, and serine-rich regions characteristic of Zip3 family proteins.

claim: Vilya is required for meiotic double-strand break formation.
source: Vilya is required for meiotic DSB formation, perhaps as a consequence of its interaction with the DSB accessory protein Mei-P22
evidence: Demonstrated through immunofluorescence showing absence of γH2AV foci in vilya mutants, rescue experiments with X-ray treatment, and genetic analysis showing rescue of okra mutant phenotypes.

claim: Vilya localizes to DSB sites that will mature into crossovers.
source: Vilya is required for meiotic DSB formation, perhaps as a consequence of its interaction with the DSB accessory protein Mei-P22, and localizes to those DSB sites that will mature into crossovers.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence showing Vilya3XHA foci colocalizing with γH2AV marks and immuno-EM showing Vilya at recombination nodules.

claim: In early pachytene, Vilya localizes along the central region of the synaptonemal complex and to discrete foci.
source: In early pachytene Vilya localizes along the central region of the synaptonemal complex and to discrete foci.
evidence: Demonstrated through structured illumination microscopy showing both linear tracks and discrete foci of Vilya3XHA within the central region of the SC.

claim: The accumulation of Vilya at foci is dependent on DSB formation.
source: The accumulation of Vilya at foci is dependent on DSB formation.
evidence: Shown by experiments where Vilya3XHA fails to form discrete foci in mei-P22 and mei-W68 mutants that cannot form DSBs.

claim: Vilya is a component of recombination nodules.
source: Immuno-electron microscopy demonstrates that Vilya is a component of recombination nodules, which mark the sites of crossover formation.
evidence: Demonstrated through immuno-EM showing gold particles labeling Vilya3XHA at electron-dense recombination nodule structures.

claim: Vilya links the mechanism of DSB formation to either the selection of DSBs that will become crossovers or to the actual process of crossing over.
source: Thus Vilya links the mechanism of DSB formation to either the selection of those DSBs that will become crossovers or to the actual process of crossing over.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the dual role of Vilya in DSB formation and its localization at crossover sites.

claim: Crossovers are formed within the context of the synaptonemal complex.
source: Crossovers are formed within the context of the synaptonemal complex (SC), a highly conserved proteinaceous structure formed between homologs during early meiotic prophase (Zickler and Kleckner, 1999; Page and Hawley, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: In Drosophila, DSBs are formed after full-length SC is constructed.
source: However, in flies (McKim et al., 1998; Jang et al., 2003) and worms (Dernburg et al., 1998), SC formation is not dependent on DSB formation, and in fact, DSBs are formed after full-length SC is constructed.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies in flies and worms.

claim: DSBs are induced by the evolutionarily conserved topoisomerase-like protein Spo11.
source: Although DSBs are induced by the evolutionarily conserved topoisomerase-like protein Spo11 (Keeney et al., 1997), many poorly conserved accessory proteins have been identified that are required either to facilitate the formation of the DSBs themselves or position the DSBs within the euchromatin (de Massy, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In most organisms, the number of DSBs far exceeds the number of crossover events.
source: In most organisms the number of DSBs far exceeds the number of crossover events (de Massy, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation and specific examples given for mice and flies.

claim: The ratio of DSBs to crossovers is 10 to one in mice.
source: For example, the ratio of DSBs to crossovers is 10 to one in mice (Moens et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citation to Moens et al., 2002.

claim: In flies, there are at least three times more DSBs than there are crossovers.
source: while in flies there are at least three times more DSBs than there are crossovers (Lindsley et al., 1977; Mehrotra and McKim, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lindsley et al., 1977 and Mehrotra and McKim, 2006.

claim: Zip3 was first identified in yeast.
source: Zip3 was first identified in yeast (Ouspenski et al., 1999; Agarwal and Roeder, 2000), and homologs have now been identified in many other model organisms.
evidence: Supported by citations to the original yeast studies.

claim: There are two subgroups within the Zip3 family: the Zip3/RNF212 group and the Hei10 group.
source: Recently it has been suggested that there are two subgroups within the Zip3 family: the Zip3/RNF212 group and the Hei10 group (Chelysheva et al., 2012; De Muyt et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: All members within both Zip3 subgroups are required for the formation of crossovers.
source: All the members within both subgroups are required for the formation of crossovers and are similar in terms of protein structure; they contain a RING-type zinc finger domain, an internal coiled-coil domain, and a C-terminal domain that tends to be serine rich (Reynolds et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reynolds et al., 2013.

claim: Zip3/RNF212 group members appear to act solely as SUMO E3 ligases.
source: Zip3/RNF212 group members appear to act solely as SUMO E3 ligases, whereas some members of the Hei10 group appear to possess both ubiquitin E3 ligase and SUMO E3 ligase activity.
evidence: Supported by subsequent citations to biochemical studies on yeast Zip3 and human Hei10.

claim: Yeast Zip3 has SUMO E3 ligase activity in vitro.
source: Yeast Zip3, which is required to regulate SUMO modification along meiotic chromosomes, has SUMO E3 ligase activity in vitro (Cheng et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to Cheng et al., 2006.

claim: Human Hei10 has ubiquitin E3 ligase activity in vitro.
source: Conversely, human Hei10 has been shown biochemically to have ubiquitin E3 ligase activity in vitro (Toby et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Toby et al., 2003.

claim: Mouse Hei10 may function as a SUMO E3 ligase.
source: However, recent studies suggest that mouse Hei10 may also function as a SUMO E3 ligase (Strong and Schimenti, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Strong and Schimenti, 2010.

claim: Prior to this study, homologs for most proteins required for DSB fate determination had not been identified in Drosophila.
source: Prior to this study, homologs for most of the proteins required for this process in other organisms (Msh4/Msh5 (Yokoo et al., 2012), RNF212, Hei10 (Strong and Schimenti, 2010), Mlh1/Mlh3) had not been identified in Drosophila.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to the current study, with citations.

claim: Mei-P22 is a DSB accessory protein that localizes to discrete foci prior to DSB formation.
source: Mei-P22 is a relatively small protein that localizes to discrete foci prior to DSB formation, is required for DSB formation, and partially colocalizes with γH2AV (Liu et al., 2002, Mehrotra and McKim, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on Mei-P22.

claim: Vilya is the first recombination nodule protein component identified in Drosophila.
source: Indeed, we show that Vilya is a component of recombination nodules (RNs) by immuno-electron microscopy (immuno-EM), making it the first RN protein component identified in Drosophila.
evidence: This is stated explicitly in the introduction and supported by the immuno-EM data presented in the results.

claim: Drosophila females provide an excellent system to analyze early events of the first meiotic division because egg chambers are arranged according to developmental age.
source: Drosophila females provide an excellent system to analyze the progression of very early events of the first meiotic division because egg chambers within each ovariole of the ovary are arranged according to developmental age (King et al., 1956).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Drosophila system, supported by citation.

claim: The germline stem cell divides to produce a cystoblast, which undergoes four rounds of incomplete cell division to produce a 16-cell interconnected cyst.
source: In region 1, the germline stem cell (GSC) divides to produce a cystoblast, which undergoes four rounds of incomplete cell division to produce a 16-cell interconnected cyst.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila oogenesis.

claim: Known components of the Drosophila SC associate with centromeres in early premeiotic divisions and are required for pairing and clustering of centromeres.
source: Known components of the Drosophila SC, which are thought to be exclusively on meiotic chromosomes, associate with centromeres in the early premeiotic divisions and are required for the pairing and clustering of centromeres that begins at the eight-cell cyst (Takeo et al., 2011; Tanneti et al., 2011; Christophorou et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Zygotene of prophase I begins in the 16-cell cyst in region 2A.
source: Zygotene of prophase I begins in the 16-cell cyst, in region 2A, which is best defined by the presence of additional punctate SC staining throughout the euchromatin in up to four nuclei.
evidence: This describes the developmental staging in Drosophila oogenesis.

claim: In Drosophila, meiotic DSBs are formed by Mei-W68 after the SC is fully formed.
source: In Drosophila, meiotic DSBs are formed by the Spo11 homolog, Mei-W68, after the SC is fully formed (McKim and Hayashi-Hagihara, 1998; Mehrotra and McKim, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DSBs can be visualized in Drosophila by the rapid phosphorylation of the histone 2A variant (γH2AV) at DSB sites.
source: DSBs can be visualized in Drosophila by the rapid phosphorylation of the histone 2A variant (γH2AV) at DSB sites that occur in all 16 nuclei within the cyst (in both the pro-oocytes and surrounding nurse cells) in region 2A (Mehrotra and McKim, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mehrotra and McKim, 2006.

claim: The mutation in vilya826 is a C-T transition that results in a premature stop codon.
source: This fully recessive mutation resulted in a C–T transition within a previously uncharacterized gene known as CG2709 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and is predicted to truncate the protein 24 amino acids from the end (R213STOP)
evidence: This is data from sequencing the mutant allele.

claim: A transgene expressing vilya3XHA in the germline fully rescued the chromosome segregation defect in vilya826 homozygotes.
source: A transgene construct expressing a tagged version of the wild-type vilya gene (denoted vilya3XHA) in the germline fully rescued the chromosome segregation defect seen in vilya826 homozygotes (Figure 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by genetic complementation experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: vilya826 is a null allele.
source: In addition, the meiotic nondisjunction phenotype of vilya826 homozygotes was very similar to Df(vilya)/vilya826 transheterozygotes, suggesting that vilya826 is a null allele (Figure 1B).
evidence: Inferred from the similarity of phenotypes between homozygotes and transheterozygotes with a deficiency.

claim: Vilya contains a Cys3HisCys4 RING domain.
source: vilya is predicted to encode a protein with several identifiable domains. In the N-terminal region there is a Cys3HisCys4 Really Interesting New Gene (RING) domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Based on protein sequence analysis and domain prediction.

claim: RING domains are structural domains that bind two zinc cations and are typically found in E3 ligases.
source: RING domains are structural domains that bind two zinc cations and are typically found in E3 ligases (Metzger et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Vilya contains a predicted coiled-coil domain in the middle of the protein.
source: In the middle of the protein there is a predicted coiled-coil domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) (Lupas et al., 1991).
evidence: Based on computational prediction using the COILS program.

claim: Coiled-coil domains are often involved in protein-protein interactions and are commonly found in proteins that localize to the SC.
source: Coiled-coil domains are often involved in protein–protein interactions and are commonly found in proteins that localize to the SC (Sym et al., 1993; Page and Hawley, 2004; Smolikov et al., 2009; Collins et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The C-terminal region of Vilya is serine rich, with the last quarter being approximately 25% serines.
source: Additionally, the C-terminal region of Vilya is serine rich, with the last quarter of the protein being approximately 25% serines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Based on protein sequence analysis.

claim: vilya826 oocytes show no defects in centromere pairing/clustering compared to wild type.
source: Unlike mutants that fail to pair and/or cluster their centromeres properly and thus display greater than three centromere foci (Takeo et al., 2011), oocytes homozygous for vilya826 showed no defects in centromere pairing/clustering when compared to wild type.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence analysis of CID foci shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: vilya826 is not defective in euchromatic homolog pairing as assayed by FISH for the X chromosome.
source: Similarly, vilya826 was not defective in euchromatic homolog pairing as assayed for the X chromosome by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH).
evidence: Demonstrated by FISH analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Immunofluorescence analysis did not reveal defects in the ability of the SC protein Corolla to localize properly in vilya826 germaria.
source: Moreover, immunofluorescence analysis of early pachytene nuclei did not reveal defects in the ability of the SC protein Corolla to localize properly in vilya826 germaria (Figure 1D–a,b).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence imaging.

claim: No defects were detected in timing or localization of the TF SC protein C(3)G or Orb in vilya826.
source: As well, we did not detect defects in timing or localization of the TF SC protein, C(3)G, or Orb, a cytoplasmic marker for oocyte determination (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence analysis.

claim: The formation of DSBs is greatly reduced in vilya826 and Df/vilya826 oocytes.
source: However, the formation of DSBs, as assayed with an antibody recognizing γH2AV, was greatly reduced in vilya826 and Df/vilya826 oocytes.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence analysis of γH2AV foci shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: vilya826 and Df/vilya826 females show an almost complete absence of γH2AV staining in region 2A cysts, similar to mei-W68 and mei-P22.
source: We found that unlike wild-type and c(3)G females, where γH2AV foci are readily observed in region 2A cysts, vilya826 and Df/vilya826 females show an almost complete absence of γH2AV staining, similar to mei-W68 and mei-P22.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The defect in DSB formation in vilya826 is not caused by a delay in DSB formation.
source: This defect is not caused by a delay in DSB formation, as no γH2AV foci were detected in later stages of pachytene in the germarium (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by examining later stages of pachytene.

claim: The near complete absence of γH2AV foci in vilya826 oocytes is not due to an inability to modify the histone at DSB sites.
source: The near complete absence of the γH2AV foci in vilya826 oocytes was also not due to an inability of vilya826 to modify the histone at DSB sites, as γH2AV was detected in vilya826 oocytes when DSBs were artificially induced by X-ray treatment (Figure 1D,C).
evidence: Demonstrated by X-ray treatment experiments.

claim: Germline expression of vilya3XHA rescues DSB formation in vilya mutant females.
source: Finally, the failure to induce DSBs in vilya mutant females is solely due to the lack of functional Vilya because germline expression of vilya3XHA is able to rescue DSB formation (Figure 1D–d).
evidence: Demonstrated by rescue experiments with the transgene.

claim: vilya826 rescues the fertility defect of the DSB repair-deficient mutant okra.
source: However, in the vilya826 okra double mutant, the fertility was similar to vilya826 alone, averaging 14.4 and 16.3 progeny per female, respectively, and the rate of X and 4th chromosome nondisjunction in the double mutant was similar to the vilya826 single mutant (Figure 2A). Therefore, the reduction of DSBs due to the vilya mutation resulted in the rescue of fertility (about 30% as fertile as wild type) caused by the okra mutation.
evidence: Demonstrated by genetic analysis of double mutants.

claim: vilya826 rescues the karyosome defect seen in okra mutants.
source: vilya826 was also able to rescue the karyosome defect seen in okra mutants (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence analysis of karyosome structure.

claim: vilya826 shows a complete failure of recombination in two intervals spanning the majority of the X chromosome.
source: An analysis of meiotic recombination in two intervals that span the majority of the X chromosome shows a complete failure of recombination in vilya826 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by genetic recombination assays.

claim: The frequency of recombination across the entire 3rd chromosome is reduced over 50-fold in vilya826 compared to wild type.
source: We also analyzed the frequency of recombination across the entire 3rd chromosome and found that the frequency of recombination was reduced over 50-fold in vilya826 compared to wild type (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by genetic recombination assays.

claim: During early pachytene, Vilya3XHA localizes to the central region of the SC in both linear stretches and discrete foci.
source: We find that during early pachytene, Vilya3XHA localizes to the central region of the SC in both linear stretches and discrete foci (Figure 3A-a).
evidence: Demonstrated by structured illumination microscopy.

claim: Vilya3XHA linear tracks appear within the central region of the SC, between the two lateral sides.
source: The Vilya3XHA linear tracks appear within the central region of the SC, as the fluorescence is seen in between the two lateral sides of the SC using an antibody that localizes to the C terminus of the TF protein C(3)G (Anderson et al., 2005, Collins et al., 2014).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-localization with C(3)G antibody using structured illumination microscopy.

claim: As the cyst progresses to early/mid-pachytene, the linear tracks of Vilya become less apparent and the foci become more discrete.
source: As the cyst progresses to early/mid-pachytene, the linear tracks of Vilya become less apparent and the foci become more discrete (Figure 3A-c,d).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence analysis at different stages.

claim: Vilya3XHA foci are most abundant in region 2A with an average of 8 foci.
source: We counted the number of discrete foci throughout each stage of pachytene in the germarium and found that similar to the trend in γH2AV foci number (see Figure 1C), Vilya3XHA foci are most abundant in region 2A (average 8 foci, SD = 2)
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative analysis of foci shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Vilya3XHA foci decline gradually throughout early/mid-pachytene to an average of 4.4 in region 2B and 3.2 in region 3.
source: and then decline gradually throughout early/mid-pachytene (region 2B average 4.4, SD = 0.8). In mid-pachytene (region 3), a stage in which DSB repair is underway or complete, we still see an average of 3.2 Vilya3XHA foci (SD = 0.9)
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The persistence of Vilya3XHA at discrete foci after DSB repair has begun suggests Vilya plays a role in the completion of actual crossovers.
source: The observation that Vilya3XHA persists at discrete foci after DSB repair has begun and crossovers are forming suggests that Vilya plays a role in the completion of actual crossovers, such as in the breaking and exchange of LEs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal persistence of Vilya foci.

claim: The majority (92%) of Vilya3XHA foci in nuclei with five clearly identifiable chromosome arms localize to one strand.
source: The majority (22/24) of the SC between homologous chromosome arms were associated with only one Vilya3XHA focus.
evidence: Demonstrated by 3D analysis and tracing of SC shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The number of Vilya3XHA foci in early/mid-pachytene oocytes correspond well to the known number and position of crossover events in flies.
source: Thus the number of Vilya3XHA foci in early/mid-pachytene oocytes are consistently found and correspond well to the known number and position of crossover events in flies, with each stretch of euchromatic SC between homologous chromosome arms primarily containing one focus (Lindsley et al., 1977).
evidence: This is an inference based on the quantitative analysis of foci distribution and comparison to known crossover frequencies.

claim: Vilya3XHA foci were found exclusively within the euchromatic SC, with no foci detected in the heterochromatic SC.
source: In addition, as is seen in the images in Figures 3C-a,b and corresponding Video 1, the Vilya3XHA foci were found exclusively within the euchromatic SC, and no Vilya3XHA foci were detected in the less-defined heterochromatic SC.
evidence: Demonstrated by 3D visualization and tracing of SC.

claim: No colocalization of Vilya3XHA foci with CID (CENP-A homolog) was detected throughout early/mid-pachytene.
source: Consistent with this observation we failed to detect any colocalization of Vilya3XHA foci with the histone variant (CID, the CENP-A homolog) that localizes in the pericentromeric heterochromatin throughout early/mid-pachytene (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence co-localization analysis.

claim: Gold particles localizing to electron-dense recombination nodules were frequently observed in immuno-EM analysis of vilya3XHA-expressing oocytes.
source: We performed immuno-EM using a secondary antibody labeled with gold particles on oocytes expressing vilya3XHA. In the analysis of 50 nm sections we frequently observed gold particles localizing to electron-dense RNs.
evidence: Demonstrated by immuno-EM shown in Figure 4.

claim: Gold particles were detected throughout the entire central region of the SC, as well as small clusters in small electron-dense regions.
source: In addition to the localization at RNs, we were able to detect gold particles throughout the entire central region of the SC, as well as small clusters of gold particles in what appear to be small electron-dense regions of the central region (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated by immuno-EM.

claim: The discrete Vilya3XHA foci detected by immunofluorescence correspond to the EM structure of recombination nodules.
source: From these studies, we conclude that the discrete Vilya3XHA foci we detect within the central region of the SC by immunofluorescence correspond to the EM structure of the RNs, and/or their precursors, and are the sites of crossing over.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the immuno-EM data.

claim: In the absence of mei-P22 or mei-W68, Vilya3XHA is found exclusively and uniformly throughout the central region of the SC and fails to localize to discrete foci.
source: Unlike in the presence of one wild-type copy of mei-P22 (Figure 5A) or mei-W68 (Figure 5B), in the homozygous mutant backgrounds (Figure 5C,D), Vilya3XHA is found exclusively and uniformly throughout the central region of the SC and fails to localize to discrete foci
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence analysis in mutant backgrounds.

claim: DSB formation is required for the localization of Vilya3XHA to discrete foci but not for linear localization to the central region of the SC.
source: indicating that DSB formation is required for the localization of Vilya3XHA to discrete foci but not for the linear localization to the central region of the SC.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the localization patterns in DSB-deficient mutants.

claim: 60.5% of Vilya3XHA foci are closely associated with γH2AV in early pachytene nuclei.
source: We find that 60.5% of the Vilya3XHA foci are closely associated with γH2AV (49 of the 81 Vilya3XHA foci from 11 early pachytene nuclei).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative immunofluorescence co-localization analysis.

claim: The degree of association between Vilya3XHA and γH2AV modification at DSB sites is significant and cannot be explained by coincidence.
source: In the 11 early pachytene oocytes that showed an association frequency of 60.5%, only 8.6% (7 of the 81 Vilya3XHA foci) remained associated after rotation of the Vilya3XHA channel, suggesting the observed degree of association between Vilya3XHA foci and the γH2AV modification cannot be explained by coincidence (p < 0.0001, binomial test).
evidence: Demonstrated by randomized control experiments and statistical analysis.

claim: In the absence of DSB repair (spnB mutant), the number of Vilya3XHA foci in region 3 increases from an average of 3.2 to 7.5.
source: We find that in the absence of DSB repair, the number of Vilya3XHA foci in region 3 increases from an average of 3.2 (SD = 0.9) in an otherwise wild-type background (Figure 3B) to 7.5 (SD = 1.6, n = 10 oocytes).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative analysis in spnB mutant background.

claim: The frequency of Vilya3XHA foci associated with γH2AV marks in spnB mutant is 68%, comparable to early pachytene in wild-type background.
source: The frequency of Vilya3XHA foci associated with γH2AV marks was 68% (51 of the 75 Vilya3XHA foci in 10 oocytes), comparable to the 60.5% seen in early pachytene when DSB repair is progressing normally (p = 0.93, binomial test) (Figure 6B and 6B-b').
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative co-localization analysis with statistical comparison.

claim: In the absence of C(3)G, Vilya3XHA is able to localize to discrete foci that are often associated with γH2AV marks.
source: As shown in Figure 7, we find that in the absence of C(3)G, Vilya3XHA is able to localize in early pachytene oocytes to discrete foci that are often associated with γH2AV marks (75% of Vilya3XHA foci, 34 of 45, colocalize with γH2AV marks in 14 oocyte nuclei analyzed).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence analysis in c(3)G mutant background.

claim: Vilya3XHA foci are reduced in number in c(3)G mutant compared to wild type in region 2A.
source: As the number of DSBs in oocytes of a c(3)G mutant are reduced to 15–20% of normal (Mehrotra and McKim, 2006), as expected, Vilya3XHA foci are also reduced in number compared to wild type in region 2A (an average of 3.2 Vilya3XHA foci per oocyte compared to 8.0 in wild type).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantitative analysis in c(3)G mutant background, with reference to previous studies on DSB levels.

claim: Linear Vilya3XHA staining was never observed in the absence of c(3)G.
source: In addition, we never observed linear Vilya3XHA staining in the absence of c(3)G, indicating that the SC is required to localize Vilya to the central element but not to DSBs.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence analysis in c(3)G mutant background.

claim: The SC is required to localize Vilya to the central element but not to DSBs.
source: In addition, we never observed linear Vilya3XHA staining in the absence of c(3)G, indicating that the SC is required to localize Vilya to the central element but not to DSBs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the localization patterns in c(3)G mutant.

claim: Exogenous DSBs induced by X-ray can recruit Vilya3XHA to discrete foci in mei-W68 mutant background.
source: We find that in some instances, Vilya3XHA foci could be detected at γH2AV marks (Figure 8).
evidence: Demonstrated by X-ray treatment experiments in mei-W68 mutant background.

claim: The ability of X-ray-induced lesions to form discrete Vilya3XHA foci suggests Vilya is playing an active role in the processing of DSBs.
source: Although we do not know at this time whether the X-ray-induced DSBs that recruit Vilya3XHA to them can be processed into crossovers, the ability of X-ray-induced lesions to concentrate and form discrete Vilya3XHA foci at some of them suggests that Vilya is playing an active role in the processing of DSBs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the X-ray recruitment experiments.

claim: Vilya and Mei-P22 strongly interact in the yeast two-hybrid system.
source: In the yeast two-hybrid system, we found that Vilya and Mei-P22 strongly interact as assayed on the reporter plate (Figure 9).
evidence: Demonstrated by yeast two-hybrid assay.

claim: Vilya826 can interact with Mei-P22, although this interaction appears weaker than with full-length Vilya.
source: We determined that the Vilya826 form of the protein could also interact with Mei-P22 in this assay, although this interaction appeared to be weaker than with full-length Vilya when controlled for plating.
evidence: Demonstrated by yeast two-hybrid assay shown in Figure 9.

claim: Mei-P22103 can interact with Vilya, albeit to a lesser extent for Vilya826.
source: We found that this mutation, which abolishes Mei-P22 function and DSB formation in vivo, is still able to bind to both Vilya, and Vilya826, albeit to a lesser extent for Vilya826 when controlling for plating.
evidence: Demonstrated by yeast two-hybrid assay shown in Figure 9.

claim: Mutations in any of the key residues in the RING domain ablate the ability of Vilya to interact with Mei-P22.
source: Each of the mutations ablates the ability of Vilya to interact with Mei-P22 (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by yeast two-hybrid assays with RING domain mutants.

claim: The failure of RING domain mutants to interact with Mei-P22 is not due to altered protein expression levels or degradation.
source: The failure of the RING domain mutants to interact with Mei-P22 is not due to altered protein expression levels or degradation, as we do not observe any obvious differences in the amount or size of the RING domain mutant proteins compared to wild type (Figure 9—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis.

claim: A functional RING domain within the Vilya protein is critical for Vilya and Mei-P22 interaction.
source: These studies, however, do suggest that a functional RING domain within the Vilya protein is critical for Vilya and Mei-P22 interaction.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the RING domain mutant studies.

claim: Vilya and Mei-P22 likely interact in vivo.
source: Based on these studies, Vilya and Mei-P22 likely interact in vivo, and their interaction is dependent on the RING domain of Vilya.
evidence: This is an inference based on the yeast two-hybrid data.

claim: Mei-P22 localization is anticipated to not be dependent on Vilya.
source: Previous studies using the expression construct hsp83:mei-P223XHA have shown that Mei-P223XHA localizes to discrete foci, which are found on chromatin closely associated with the SC and are not dependent on DSB formation (Liu et al., 2002). Therefore, we anticipate that Mei-P22 localization is also not dependent on Vilya.
evidence: This is an inference based on previous studies showing Mei-P22 localization is independent of DSB formation.

claim: Vilya may have additional functions at the DSB site that are independent from Mei-P22.
source: The persistence of Vilya3XHA at discrete foci into early/mid-pachytene, and the absence of Mei-P223XHA staining at this stage (Liu et al., 2002; Mehrotra and McKim, 2006), suggests that Vilya may have additional functions at the DSB site, such as in crossing over, that are independent from Mei-P22.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal differences in localization patterns.

claim: Mei-P22 acts upstream of Vilya and recruits Vilya and Mei-W68.
source: Based on these observations, along with the finding that Mei-P22 and Vilya interact in a yeast two-hybrid assay, we propose that Mei-P22 acts upstream of Vilya, and recruits Vilya and Mei-W68, which catalyzes DSBs.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the genetic and biochemical data.

claim: Only those DSBs that recruit sufficient Vilya to form foci are converted into crossovers.
source: Our model further suggests that only those DSBs that recruit sufficient Vilya to form foci are converted into crossovers and can be visualized by the discrete prominent foci seen in early/mid pachytene.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on observations in budding yeast and the localization data.

claim: Differential enrichment of Zip3 at DSBs positively biases the DSB toward the crossover pathway in budding yeast.
source: We base this proposal on the observation in budding yeast that the differential enrichment of Zip3 at DSBs positively biases the DSB toward the crossover pathway (Serrentino et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge from yeast studies, supported by citation.

claim: Exogenous DSBs have the ability to recruit or concentrate Vilya.
source: We know from our studies that exogenous DSBs have the ability to recruit or concentrate Vilya to a subset of them
evidence: Demonstrated by X-ray treatment experiments.

claim: In the absence of SC, there appears to be a failure to maintain Vilya3XHA at discrete foci in early/mid-pachytene oocytes.
source: in the absence of SC there appears to be a failure to maintain Vilya3XHA at discrete foci in early/mid-pachytene oocytes
evidence: Demonstrated by analysis in c(3)G mutant background.

claim: Vilya plays an active role at the sites of crossing over.
source: Together, these data suggest that Vilya plays an active role at the sites of crossing over.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence including localization, immuno-EM, and X-ray recruitment.

claim: DIOPT predicts that Vilya is orthologous to S. cerevisiae Zip3 and C. elegans Zhp-3.
source: DIOPT, the Drosophila RNAi Screening Center Integrative Ortholog Prediction Tools (Hu, et al., 2011), predicts that Vilya is orthologous to S. cerevisiae Zip3 (also known as Cst9) and C. elegans Zhp-3
evidence: This is based on computational ortholog prediction.

claim: Evolutionarily, Vilya is more closely related to the Zip3-like members than Hei10 members.
source: This analysis suggests that evolutionarily Vilya is more closely related to the Zip3-like members than Hei10 members.
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Vilya has a putative SUMO-interacting motif and three putative RXL cyclin-binding domains.
source: In addition to these three domains, Vilya also has a putative SUMO-interacting motif (SUMO-IM) and three putative RXL cyclin-binding domains that are also common to Zip3 family members (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) (Cheng et al., 2006; Ward et al., 2007; De Muyt et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on protein sequence analysis and comparison to known motifs in Zip3 family members.

claim: No interaction was detected between Vilya and Drosophila Ubc9 in a yeast two-hybrid assay.
source: Although we have not specifically determined whether the SUMO-IM and RXL motifs in Vilya are required for its function, in preliminary studies we have not been able to detect an interaction between Vilya and the Drosophila Ubc9 in a yeast two-hybrid assay.
evidence: This is negative data from preliminary experiments.

claim: SUMOylation of proteins at the SC in Drosophila oocytes has not been detected using an antibody to Drosophila SUMO.
source: Nor have we been able to identify SUMOylation of proteins at the SC in Drosophila oocytes using an antibody to Drosophila SUMO (Abgent AP1287b, San Diego, CA).
evidence: This is negative data from immunofluorescence experiments.

claim: There is no evidence that Vilya possesses SUMO E3 ligase activity or that SUMOylation plays a role at the SC in Drosophila.
source: Therefore, although structurally Vilya bears a strong resemblance to the Zip3 family, we have no evidence Vilya possess SUMO E3 ligase activity, interacts directly with an E2 enzyme, or that SUMOylation plays a role at the SC in Drosophila at this time.
evidence: This is a statement about the current lack of evidence for SUMO E3 ligase activity.

claim: Vilya's dynamic localization pattern is similar to C. elegans Zhp-3, mouse RNF212, and Arabidopsis and rice Hei10.
source: Moreover, similar dynamic localization patterns have been seen for C. elegans Zhp-3, mouse RNF212, and Arabidopsis and rice Hei10 (Jantsch et al., 2004; Bhalla et al., 2008; Chelysheva et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2012; Reynolds et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison to known localization patterns in other organisms, supported by citations.

claim: In the absence of meiotic recombination initiation in C. elegans and mice, Zhp-3 and RNF212 localize along the SC but fail to coalesce into discrete foci.
source: In the absence of meiotic recombination initiation in C. elegans (Bhalla et al., 2008) and mice (Reynolds et al., 2013), Zhp-3 and RNF212, respectively, were also found to localize along the SC, albeit the SC of nonhomologous chromosomes in mice, and failed to coalesce into discrete foci.
evidence: This is established knowledge from studies in other organisms, supported by citations.

claim: Vilya has a unique function not found in any other Zip3 family member: being required for meiotic DSB formation.
source: Although Vilya clearly has a unique function not found in any other Zip3 family member so far (i.e. being required for meiotic DSB formation), other unique functions for some Zip3 family members have been identified as well.
evidence: This is a comparative statement highlighting the unique role of Vilya.

claim: Zip3 in budding yeast is the only Zip3 family member required for SC assembly.
source: For example, Zip3 in budding yeast appears to be the only member required for SC assembly (Agarwal and Roeder, 2000; Bhalla et al., 2008)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Hei10 in Sordaria is uniquely required for processes involving spindle pole body dynamics.
source: and Hei10 in Sordaria is uniquely required for processes involving spindle pole body dynamics (De Muyt et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Drosophila appear to lack homologs of the meiosis-specific MutS complex.
source: Because DSB accessory proteins are highly divergent and Drosophila appear to lack homologs of the meiosis-specific MutS complex (Yokoo et al., 2012), which are required to stabilize strand invasion during crossing over, and the crossover-specific complex MutLγ, to which Zip3 family members bind
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Drosophila has found a unique way to couple the events of DSB formation to those of crossing over.
source: perhaps then it is not surprising that Drosophila has found an unique way to couple the events of DSB formation to those of crossing over.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the unique features of Vilya and the absence of certain conserved proteins in Drosophila.
